paragraphs.title: The Vision of the Two Baskets and the Distinction Between the Figs

answers: Two baskets of figs
Two temples
Two kingdoms
easy.explanation: The Lord showed Jeremiah two baskets of figs set before the temple of the Lord.
easy.q: What did the Lord show Jeremiah in his vision?

answers: In the land of the Chaldeans
Before the temple of the Lord
In the land of Egypt
easy.explanation: The baskets were set before the temple of the Lord.

answers: Very bad figs
Figs that could not be eaten
Very good figs
easy.explanation: One basket had very good figs, like figs that are first ripe.
easy.q: How is the first basket of figs described?

answers: After Jerusalem was rebuilt
After Jeconiah, Judah's princes, and the craftsmen were carried away captive
After the exiles returned
medium.explanation: The vision occurred after Nebuchadrezzar carried Jeconiah, the princes, and the carpenters and smiths to Babylon.
medium.q: After what event did Jeremiah see this vision?

answers: One had very good figs and the other had very bad figs
One had green figs and the other had ripe figs
One had many figs and the other had only a few
medium.explanation: The passage sharply contrasts the very good figs with the very bad figs.
medium.q: What was the main difference between the two baskets?

answers: Figs that ripen early and are especially desirable
Figs that are still completely unripe
Figs that have already spoiled
medium.explanation: The good figs are compared to figs that ripen first, suggesting excellent quality.
medium.q: In the KJV, what does “first ripe” mean when describing the figs?

answers: He did not yet know the meaning of the vision
The figs had nothing to do with the exile
The baskets were only decorations for the temple
challenge.explanation: Jeremiah first reports what he saw, and the Lord explains its meaning afterward.
challenge.q: What can be inferred from Jeremiah describing the baskets before receiving the Lord's explanation?

answers: Those living in Egypt
The carpenters and smiths
The remnant left in Jerusalem
challenge.explanation: The KJV says that Nebuchadrezzar carried away the carpenters and smiths to Babylon.
challenge.q: Which group is specifically mentioned among those carried away to Babylon?

answers: That the two kinds of figs were nearly alike
That the difference was only in their size
That the good figs were very good and the evil figs were so bad they could not be eaten
challenge.explanation: The repeated wording emphasizes the extreme contrast between the two kinds of figs.
challenge.q: What is emphasized by Jeremiah's repeated description of the figs?

paragraphs.title: The Babylonian Exiles as the Good Figs

answers: The captivity of Judah sent to the land of the Chaldeans
Zedekiah and his princes
Those living in Egypt
easy.explanation: The Lord compares the good figs to the people of Judah whom He sent into the land of the Chaldeans.
easy.q: Whom do the good figs represent?

answers: Destroy them
Set His eyes upon them for good
Leave them in Egypt
easy.explanation: The Lord said, “I will set mine eyes upon them for good.”
easy.q: What did the Lord promise to do for the exiles?

answers: An heart to know Him
Rule over Babylon
New baskets of figs
easy.explanation: The Lord promised to give them an heart to know Him.
easy.q: What would the Lord give the exiles?

answers: Destruction, famine, and captivity
Return to the land, building, and planting
Leaving the land, war, and cursing
medium.explanation: The Lord promised to bring them again to the land, build them up, and plant them.
medium.q: Which sequence correctly states the Lord's promises to the exiles?

answers: I will remove them from the land
I will send them to war
I will establish them securely and keep them in the land
medium.explanation: Planting them contrasts with plucking them up and indicates restoration and stability.
medium.q: In this passage, what does “I will plant them” indicate?

answers: They would know the Lord and return to Him with their whole heart
They would know the Lord but turn away from Him
They would return to the land without any relationship with the Lord
medium.explanation: The passage joins receiving a heart to know the Lord with returning to Him wholeheartedly.
medium.q: What connection does the passage make between knowing the Lord and returning to Him?

answers: Because they would disappear from the land
Because the Lord would watch over them, restore them, and build them up
Because they would remain permanently in Babylon
challenge.explanation: The good figs symbolize the Lord's favor, protection, restoration, and renewal of the exiles.
challenge.q: Why is the image of good figs appropriate for the promises made to the exiles?

answers: They would be His people, and He would be their God
They would be His enemies, and He would drive them away
They would cease to know Him
challenge.explanation: The Lord says, “They shall be my people, and I will be their God.”
challenge.q: What change in the relationship between the Lord and His people is described?

answers: It would be only partial
It would mean only returning to the land
It would be complete and wholehearted
challenge.explanation: The phrase indicates a sincere and complete return to the Lord, not merely a change of location.
challenge.q: What does the phrase “with their whole heart” teach about their return to the Lord?

paragraphs.title: The Bad Figs and the Judgment of Those Who Remained

answers: The captivity of Judah in Babylon
Zedekiah, his princes, the remnant of Jerusalem, and those living in Egypt
The carpenters and smiths alone
easy.explanation: The evil figs represent Zedekiah, his princes, the remnant of Jerusalem, and those dwelling in Egypt.
easy.q: Whom do the evil figs represent?

answers: The sword, the famine, and the pestilence
Rain, peace, and abundance
Building, planting, and restoration
easy.explanation: The Lord said He would send the sword, the famine, and the pestilence among them.
easy.q: What judgments would come upon the people represented by the evil figs?

answers: As a blessing and an honor
As a reproach and a proverb
As first-ripe fruit and food
easy.explanation: They would be a reproach, a proverb, a taunt, and a curse.
easy.q: How would they be regarded among the kingdoms of the earth?

answers: Honor and praise
Shame and disgrace
Rest and peace
medium.explanation: A reproach is a cause of shame or disgrace, fitting the words “a proverb,” “a taunt,” and “a curse.”
medium.q: In the KJV, what does “a reproach” mean in this context?

answers: The good figs receive restoration, while the evil figs suffer judgment and are consumed from the land
Both groups receive exactly the same treatment
The evil figs are rebuilt, while the good figs are destroyed
medium.explanation: The good figs receive God's favor and restoration, while the evil figs face judgment and removal.
medium.q: What is the difference between the outcome for the good figs and the evil figs?

answers: They are built and planted again
They suffer the sword, the famine, and the pestilence
They return to the Lord with their whole heart
medium.explanation: Their judgment through war, famine, and pestilence leads to their disgrace among the kingdoms.
medium.q: What causes the people represented by the evil figs to become a reproach and a proverb?

answers: Exile has the same meaning for every group
The groups differ according to God's judgment and their expected outcome, not merely according to their location
There is no real difference between the good and evil figs
challenge.explanation: The Babylonian exiles receive promises of good, while Zedekiah and the others receive a sentence of judgment.
challenge.q: What can be inferred from the contrast between verses 5–7 and verses 8–10?

answers: Until they are destroyed or removed from the land
Until they are rebuilt in the land
Until they return to the Lord with their whole heart
challenge.explanation: The phrase describes the continuation of judgment until they are consumed from the land.
challenge.q: What does the phrase “till they be consumed from off the land” mean in context?

answers: Because the passage includes them among those appointed to judgment
Because they were among the exiles sent to the land of the Chaldeans
Because they would become the good figs
challenge.explanation: The passage explicitly includes those dwelling in Egypt among the people whom the Lord would judge.
challenge.q: Why are those living in the land of Egypt included among the evil figs?
